title: Not sound-proof, but good enough for office use.
text:
I knew right away that these would be my office headphones. I have a mechanical keyboard that I use at work, and the office I work in is semi-open. There's a *lot* of noise coming every-which-way. These are a much-needed accessory to my work productivity, as I'm easily distracted by things in my periphery, whether visually or auditory.

The presentation is great. The box is very high quality, reminiscent of the recent Samsung Galaxy device boxes. A smooth matte feel with gloss--weirdly pristine. The box slides out of the slipcover and you get the headphones already in the case. What I like is that they're folded, and there's even a little sheet underneath the phones that always reminds you how to put them back in. Also included is a 3.5mm cable in case you don't want to use Bluetooth, a charging cable, and an adapter. The case is nice, but as I keep mine at work I can't testify to its durability. There's a thin mesh net on the backside in case anyone needs to store one or two thin headphone accessory/-ies along. The accent colors are a nice light copper/rose gold color. I love that color; I'm glad it's getting more attention in recent years.

It didn't take long to charge the headphones, so they come with a little bit of juice. As soon as you turn them on, you get a soft beep along with a voice indicating they're turned on. Nice responsive feedback. Once I put them on I could hear the headphones working to drown out the sound; there was a thick veil of soundproofing that was draped over my ears as soon as the earpads touched them.

The first thing I did was listen to podcasts through the Pocket Casts app and .flac music through Poweramp v3. With podcasts, the difference was phenomenal. Listening to "Wait, wait... Don't tell me!" made me feel as though I were in the audience. The music was fantastic...until I tried on my other headphones which I use for music only.
I thought the bass might've been too strong with the Sony headphones, and I was right. After using even "cheaper" headphones like the Audio-Technica M50x, I could tell the Sony had too much bass. I'm not sure if that's partly because of the noise-canceling technology or what, but the bass can be toned down a bit, methinks.

I then proceeded to download the supplementary app to get the fullest suite of attributes the headphones can get. The app works well, and I didn't experience any hiccups while actually using the app. The only hiccup was when I was trying to download the update. It took *forever*. Almost an hour and it was just halfway through. I decided to bring them to work the next day and let the app sit there while updating. Thankfully, it remembers the progress, even though the app kept crashing during the update process.

There are some optimization tweaks in the app, some sound profiles to let you configure the noise cancelation level (yes, level; the noise cancelation is pure software; you can set it to drown out the most noise as possible or have no noise cancellation at all), and even a little snippet of what is currently playing through the headphones. A simple UI with all the features you need.

The first few days I used it I was active, and I kept noticing that my ears sometimes would pop depending on whether I sat down or arose quickly. Another weird thing is that when I take the headphones off, my ears sometimes need a minute or two to adjust. There's so much noise in the world! After taking the headphones off I can hear HVAC activity and my loud work neighbor who's otherwise not that loud.

I had some headphones with some touch controls before and always found them tacky. I used them once when I first got them and never again. But with these headphones, I'm always using the tap gesture to play/pause and the swipe gesture to raise or lower the volume. There are also swipe gestures to skip or go back a track, but since I never do that anyway I never use those gestures. You have to be careful with the tap; when it works, it works. But the whole surface isn't the active portion and you have to hit it right in the center. Sometimes I'm hitting my finger against my ears trying to find the spot and hurting myself in the process. I tested the gesture where you put your entire palm on the cup to turn off the noise canceling feature and let the mic allow incoming conversation, but not after the third try. I could hear the other people just fine, but I found the right hand over my ear felt awkward, and one person didn't realize I could even hear them. Putting your hand over your headphones isn't a gesture people immediately see as you paying attention to them.

The headphones are extremely lightweight and comfortable to use; I left them on for about two hours once before having to take them off. I actually was surprised with how light they were; when I got the Amazon box I didn't believe it was my headphones. It was much lighter than expected.

For my first noise-canceling headphones I'm pleased. The sound balance can be better (less bass), but they make for fantastic headphones to use at work. I wasn't sure what I was expecting with noise-canceling technology. I thought it would drown out all noises, but you still can hear the occasional mutter; it just won't be distinct.

Oh, forgot to mention the battery life. I charged it only once and have been using it for a week, at about an hour or two each day. Still going well. If you press the power button once it will tell you the battery level. AFter the initial update the voice indicator might give the wrong battery level (it did for me), but give it about ten or fifteen minutes to adjust and it will go back to normal.

title: Excellent sound, frustrating bluetooth and terrible mic
text:
Sound and noise canceling are best-of-breed, if that's all you need: this is a pretty good buy. Comfortable, charges quickly, battery lasts, and the touch control is actually fairly nice. Especially the "cover an ear to hear the outside world" "gesture", that's a stroke of brilliance.

If you want to hook up to more than one device at a time though, it's a surprisingly painful experience. Generally speaking it only connects to one thing at a time, and *does not accept connections from other devices*. So if you want to switch from your phone to your computer, you need to explicitly disconnect from the phone, then connect from the computer. And do the reverse to go back (it'll happily reconnect to your now-sleeping laptop, and will refuse to switch to your phone).
It also has a bad habit of either being (much) too quiet or (somewhat) too loud, with no volume steps in between. My phone volume is only at 20% or 30% while listening to music, and I need to go into an EQ to turn down everything so 30% isn't uncomfortably loud. And I've needed to do that for everything I've connected it to. On a PC it's fine since there's much finer-grained volume control, but wow. Frustrating.

It feels like I'm dealing with a bluetooth device from 10 years ago. Shockingly bad, especially since it's clearly software issues that could be fixed (but haven't, a full year after launch). Coupled with a $300 price tag and it's simply inexcusable.

The microphone has been covered at length on youtube - do yourself a favor and listen to to the examples. In a quiet environment it sounds like you're speaking from another room, and anywhere louder it's almost unusable. The microphone is bad enough that I'm very strongly considering returning it and getting a Bose instead, it might as well not exist.

title: Amazing ANC
text:
When I was first thinking about writing a review for this product, I was going to start picking apart the sound quality.
Then I realized, is it really fair to compare these to open-back audiophile headphones that cost four times what these do?
The answer is no. That's not what you're getting here, and that's not what these are meant to be.
These headphones (and headphones like these) have a specific use case, and it is not critical listening.
So instead, I'll review based on that use case.

The noise cancellation on these things is outstanding!
I'm typing this on a mechanical keyboard right now, and I only hear music.
To be fair, I have spent very little time listening to Bose headphones, so I would not be the best person for a direct comparison.
What I can say for sure, however, is that these work really well.

A couple of negative points:

They could be a little more comfortable for someone with a head and ears the size of mine, but I'm used to that by now.
The bass is very present, but it's a bit loose and sloppy (not tight or accurate), and mids take a definite back seat.
It is very easy to accidentally change tracks when trying to adjust the cans.

These things being mentioned, these headphones are good enough at what they do (in context of what they are meant for - private listening, airplane listening, etc.) to be worthy of a five-star review.
If there are better ANC headphones out there, I have never tried them.

Using it on my desktop provided a muddy and distorted sound, easily surpassed by any of the other 10 pairs of headphones I have. Even my desktop speakers provide a superior listening experience.

Looking at the Amazon product page now it is still difficult to find any information stating that it is not for use with those two devices. I will say though that they are VERY comfortable, easily adjustable for fit, and I like the 'desert' color which differentiates it from the typical black headphone. The fit itself is conducive to noise cancelling even without the electronic gizmos. More comfortable than my Bose unit and just as good as providing clear sound quality. title: Great headphones for a great price!
text:
I would NOT recommend these headphones for audiophiles. I'm sure they would pick it apart and have plenty of complaints. But as somebody who just wanted a pair of phones to listen to music on the commute to and from work, it works great! Deep bass, mids and highs are clear. I don't find it all that muddy, but I'm by no means an audiophile. I think the sound quality is superb for the price tag--you can't beat it. The microphone also works superbly--I use it to call people while on the train and people on the other end can hear everything the conductor announces.

The comfort level is also decent. As someone who occasionally wears glasses, the pressure does end up giving me a slight headache after 45 mins when pushing the frames into my temples. But when I wear contacts, no issues whatsoever. Comfortable to listen to music for at least a few hours (haven't tried beyond that). My ears don't get sweaty, the headband stays put, and the cord doesn't get tangled as I jam out on the train ride home.

The only downside I would say is that they're definitely not sound isolating. My boyfriend tells me that at a certain volume he can vaguely hear sounds, and then louder than that he can start to actually hear my music. So if you plan on blasting these at top volume, your neighbors might not appreciate it so much.

Overall, a great set of headphones that serve exactly the purpose that I wanted it to fulfill. Haven't had any interaction with the customer service yet, but have seen tons of raving reviews about them, so am confident that they will provide wonderful service should I need anything.

title: Surprisingly good sound .. When you take off comfort foam in ear cups :)
text:
I bought these late last year after reading some positive reviews, but even after burning in for over 40 hours per the manufacturer recommendation, I still found the sound quite muddy, flat, and just not clear.

I own several headphones - Fostex T50RP MK3, Sennheiser HD 558, Harman Kardon BT, Sony MDR-V6, Grado SR80e, and while I certainly don't expect headphones this cheap to measure up, I did expect something closer to Koss KSC75 performance, but it was far, far from that..

Over the last few months, I'd occasionally pull them out and have another listen to see if my ears or brain had adjusted to their sound... Nope...

UNTIL I pulled off the pleather covers on the ear cups, and removed the foam and VOILA, they were transformed from "ugh" to "not bad for $10!" Whereas before I literally couldn't use them ever because the sound was sooo bad to my ears, now I take them with me on short walks when I don't want to be afraid of a little sprinkle or dust or anything else taking them out but don't feeling like stuffing in-ear headphones into my ear canals...

Comfort definitely took a hit, but surprisingly, not as much as I'd have imagined - and for a short walk of an hour or less, I didn't find them uncomfortable without the pads.

Short story: love the color, simple design, single cable on right cup only, control on cord for pausing / playing, advancing to next or going back a track, and the sound is now enjoyable and very satisfactory at this price point.

title: Excellent value for a kid headphone - WORKS FOR THE PLANE
text:
I had bought a pair of JLab kid headphones for my daughter a year or so ago from Wal Mart for about $15 and they were essentially garbage. The combo of a steep rolloff of high frequencies (I'm guessing around 13Khz) and the volume limiter made them impossible to use for any kind of noisy environment like an airplane or even a car.

...These are a huge upgrade from that AND at a lower price. They have a full frequency response (which allows you to listen at lower volumes due to being able to hear detail) and the 93db volume limit allows for listening in noisy places without risk of hearing damage. They are durable for my 2 & 5 YO. The daisy chain feature is also a great bonus. Now, the overall sound quality isn't going to compare to any serious headphone (obviously) and the background noise isolation could be better but for the $$, it would be tough to find something better.

title: DURABLE, GREAT RUN TIME, GREAT SERVICE for a GREAT VALUE!
text:
With all the hype around Beats, Bose, AirPods etc. You may think a pair of $19 - $30 headphones wouldn’t compare in any meaningful way, but in my opinion you’d be wrong. Now, I’m not an audiophile, but I listen to audiobooks and podcasts constantly. For that reason, I have 2 different pairs of SoundPeats. I own the Q30’s and Q36’s and have been overwhelmingly satisfied in the following 3 ways. This does not mean that they don’t produce outstanding music quality, I just wouldn’t be the best person to give an opinion in that regard. If the following areas are important to you as they are me, you cannot go wrong with SoundPeats Products.

1. Durability - I’ve purchased other wireless earbuds at an equivalent price point and they last me, maybe 6mo before they fail. These headphones hold up to listening of 4-8hrs a day. (I’m fortunate to be able to listen while I work)

2. Battery Longevity - again, other equivalently priced headphones boast 8hr run times and last maybe 3 hrs. in real world use. These claim 8hrs and I get 6-8hrs out of them consistently even well into a year of usage.

3. Customer Service - other equivalently priced Headphones claim a lifetime warranty and if/when you end up needing it (you usually will), they are no longer in business. Not so with SoundPeats. I’ve used their customer service to replace a pair of headphones and they are excellent! I have a pair that gave a slight crackle when the wire would move. Nothing that couldn’t be dealt with and as much as I use them, it’s possible it was a result of something I had done. At any rate, they shipped me a replacement, no questions asked.

title: The best I ever had for bluetooth.
text:
I have had these since Aug 2021, almost a year, and they are going strong and still sound great even though I use them for about 4 hours at least every day. I ran out the batteries once on a long day away, and they charged up again in about an hour after I got home. They connect to everything, Computer, digital player, and TV.
The only weird thing is sometime if I turn my head to the left, and the player is in my pants pocket on the left, it will "switch" connections and glitch -- I guess the left headphone becomes "the master" then or something. This is when the player's battery is getting low. So I wear a shirt with a pocket on the chest, and put the player there, and it is much better.
The range of these is about 30 feet through walls for my computer and about 15 feet for the player. The sound never loses quality ever.
The earpiece does not "go in" to your ear it sits at the outside, so sometimes the rubber bulb gets separated from my ear a bit and loses bass but a mere push back returns it fully. They do not fall out, the ear strap works like it is supposed to, and it's very comfortable.
If I lose them, I will replace them immediately with exactly the same ones.
The price is very affordable for the quality and hassle-free use.

title: Don’t even bother. OK for podcasts in dead quiet environments. Comfortable with glasses.
text:
Bought these because they were highly rated for people who wear glasses. They’re comfy enough, but the sound quality is trash and volume is nonexistent unless you turn it all the way up and press them against your head. I decided to return them because while trying them out in public, I got out of my car in a Walmart parking lot and immediately couldn't hear them, even at full volume, just due to the ambient noise (slight breeze, traffic, semi idling across the way, etc.) They just completely got drowned out.

I bought them so I could listen to podcasts at work without disturbing others and without having to have one AirPod in, which gives me a feeling of unbalance that I was hoping not having either ear obstructed would solve. These are fine for that in a DEAD QUIET environment. At about 3/4 volume on the iPhone, I can hear clear enough and they’re not going to disturb anyone. I could have it at about 50% and other people would never know I was listening to anything. Any louder and others can hear a little buzzing. But again; as soon as you consider the air conditioning or whatever, you won't be able to hear them.

For $50, I’m not sure you can do much better. I’m interested in seeing how the more expensive brands compare. These are TERRIBLE for music. Don't even bother.

Another reviewer said these go on your cartilage (your tragus) - they do not. They go on your temple right in front of your tragus.

I wish they were just a LITTLE tighter. Maybe if I lose some weight there’ll be less fat to buffer the sound and they’ll sound better… I feel like if they were just a little tighter, the volume would increase significantly as well as the sound quality. I'm not sure how comfortable they'd be if you left them on/in for several hours, though, if they were tighter.

Overall, whether it's the technology or this exact implementation of the tech, they just don't work well.

title: Very comfortable, as advertised, and good sound quality
text:
I really like these earbuds. I use the medium-sized ear cushions. They fit me fine. I can keep them in for 5-7 hours listening to audiobooks, music or hooked to the transmitter for listening to my TV, and they do not hurt my ears. The sound quality is good for all of these activities.

I used my voice-recognition app on my Android smartphone, and it worked as well as if I didn't have these earbuds in.

The cord is only a little over 3 feet long, which is a bit short. However, this cord seems to tangle up a lot less than my other brands of earbuds.

I got the blue color, and it is a clear, bright, attractive blue.

I did not like the clamshell packaging! It is a pain to open, and having to use scissors to cut open such packaging leaves dangerously sharp edges that can easily cut the skin if one does not take extreme care to prevent it. You also need to watch out that you don't accidentally throw out the extra ear cushions which come in several sizes.

title: Pretty good utility earbuds
text:
A couple of comments about the packaging. It stinks. Designed for those store racks with hooks, the packages are understandably small, but miserable to open. I had to use shears along the very narrow ridge of the plastic bubble. It was kind of a pain, so I only did one side and fished the earbuds. It wasn’t until the dinner scraps had been dumped into the garbage can that I realized I didn’t get the Small and Large replacement Silicon ear cushions out of the package. Oh well, the Mediums fit okay, for the most part.

For what you get, I think these are overpriced.

The Medium ear cushions fit pretty well Some extraneous noise was muted. I listened some vocal and some instrumental music on Pandora and frequency response was acceptable. Since the earbuds feel comfortable, I could probably listen for several hours. I tried several YouTube videos, some of which had lousy audio, and the earbuds did a good job.

Both the earbuds and in-line microphone worked well on Skype I could hear the person I called me and they could hear me without difficulty.

I also tried an iPad speech-to-text recognition app and it worked much better than I expected it to. Belter than 90% accuracy (!) in my testing with little ambient background noise and making sure I spoke clearly and at a reasonable pace.

The cord is 3.3-feet long. I would prefer a longer cord.

Overall, I consider these to be pretty good utility earpods, but somewhat overpriced.

Jerry

title: Upgraded T10 Earbuds
text: I have the previous version of the Tranya T10 earbuds and still use them for, mainly, at the gym. I decided to buy/try the upgraded T10s before giving them as a gift. The upgraded T10s, much like the previous version, come through with easy device pairing, great sound, and plenty of battery life both in the earbuds as well as the case. The IPX7 rating ensures that any sweat or other moisture (within reason) will not degrade the earbuds. The main differences between the two versions is that the newer version does not support wireless charging and does not have a 'bass mode/boost' (replaced by 'game mode'). Charging the T10s is relatively quick with the USB-C cable and I have power to last several gym trips along with any airplane travel. The sound is balanced in my opinion....plenty of bass despite the lack of 'bass boost' in the previous version. I did find myself using the T10s for several phone calls and they performed exceptionally well. Overall, these earbuds remain a great value for the price and definitely recommend.

title: Very, Very Good
text: These in-ear headphones are very impressive.  They are durable, have lots of different sizes of ear plugs so I'm sure one of them will fit your ears perfectly.  The cord is made of a type of nylon material that won't allow you to hear the cord dragging across your shirt.  They sound very, very good, but for my taste they're a bit bass-heavy.  If some ear-thumping bass is what you like then you won't be disappointed in these.  But if you're looking for some separation between the lows, mids and highs and not wanting your bass to override everything else, then maybe you should look at a different set of headphones.  Depending on what type of music you're listening to, for instance, Lady Gaga....  then these phones will make you happy, but not so great if you're into Simon and Garfunkle.  And to really get the fantastic sound from these headphones you need to set your volume around 8 or 9 out of 10.  Anything lower and the sound gets really flat.  For half the price of these earphones, you can get a set of Skullcandy Ink'd in-ear phones that will give you across-the-board sound with enough bass to make you happy but not so much that it washes out the other ranges of music...  and you don't have to crank the Ink'd as high in volume, maybe 6-7 to get the same amount of pleasure from your music.  These SoundMagic's are very good headphones, but you can get something as good or better for a much lower price.

title: Lots to love at this price point
text:
PROS:
*Surprisingly good audio quality for a very inexpensive product.
*Headband is comfortable & washable (see below).
*The electronic components fit into sewn in "pockets" that keep the ear pieces right where you need them (and they can be moved to match your ear positions).
*Holds a charge all night.
*Does not wake bed partner
*Pairs quickly to phone

CONS:
*Volume control buttons are finicky; sometimes I have to press & hold a few times before it responds. Also they don't seem to work in all apps (for example it skips me to the next episode in Netflix rather than turning the volume up. User error maybe?)
*If you go all the way up to the highest volume it beeps once very loudly, which you don't want if you're using it for a meditation app or sleep music.
*There aren't a lot of instructions. I had to look at the pictures on the Amazon listing to figure out how in the world I'm supposed to remove the electronics for washing & replace them after (a super tedious process that took me about 20 frustrating minutes). If you sweat a lot this might be too hard to wash frequently.
*Headband arrived with a chemical smell (although soaking in Dr. Bronner's lavender soap did the trick)

OVERALL
In spite of some cons, I'm glad I bought this. I don't plan on washing it often & I can avoid the loud beep. Now I can comfortably listen to anything I like & not bother my bed partner.

title: Can’t Match The Audio Of Full Cup Headphones But Good For The Price
text:
My Bluetooth earbuds kept falling out when I tried to listen to music in bed. And, I certainly didn’t dare fall asleep while using them. I finally decided to get something more secure. This headband style “headphones” does the trick! At this price, the audio certainly doesn’t match the quality of name brand earbuds, but it works well and I will tell you that you get your money’s worth. Audio is a bit muffled and not especially crisp, but for listening to music as I fall asleep I actually found that more quiet and soothing. It takes a bait of adjusting to get the tiny speakers right next to your ears and they did not exactly line up for me, but were close enough. The speakers are tiny enough that I could sleep on the left or right side of my head with comfort. The charging port is hidden in a tiny slit and a little hard to find, but no problem if you know what to look for. These took slightly longer to pair than other Bluetooth headphones I’ve used, but did so with no problem.

Control is easy:
+ Press the middle button to power on or pause.
+ Press the left button to raise and the right button to lower the volume.
+ Hold down the right button for the next track and hold down the left button for the previous track.

Overall, this is a good headband style headphone for this price and I have really enjoyed and recommend them.

title: Decent sound quality for price, but terrible build quality
text:
I've had a pair of these for just shy of a year, and at first I loved them! They rested in my ears nicely, and barring being very active always stayed in. The sound was really great, not top of the line, but really good without spending much more. Battery last forever.

However, as time has gone on, these earbuds are showing their true colors as cheap headphones, priced much higher than they should be. It's no wonder they are always on sale. As many others have said, my number one complaint is the silicon cover on the tip (part in the ear) no longer sticks. It's completely peeled up and will completely fall off in a matter of days. With out it, the earbuds will be unbearable to use and fall out constantly. This started happening after 5 months. After continuing to deteriorate, around the 8 month mark I decided to contact JBL since these have a 1 year limited warranty, and was promptly told it doesn't cover most physical damage, even though it's from a design flaw.

I wouldn't waste your time on these. At their sale prices, you can get other products that better, and at regular price you might as well spend the extra for airpods or something else.

I have a bunch of JBL products, which is why I was draw to these initially, but I would not recommend to anyone.

title: An excellent headset-microphone for Speech Recognition
text: I purchased this microphone/headphone because I needed something that would work with Window's voice recognition software.  I had injured my hand and was unable to type for over a month, so I was going to have to dictate to my computer for a while.  It was not something I was looking forward to, since in the past I have found the software to be somewhat “glichy”, and more trouble than it was worth.  However this time I had no choice.  I first tried to use a standalone microphone, but I discovered that it was not very good at picking up my voice, and created lots of neck and back problems since I had to keep bending down to get my mouth as close to the microphone as possible.  Therefore I thought perhaps a headphone microphone would work better, and also give me more freedom of movement.  I researched many different headphone-microphones, many of which had bad reviews for being flimsy in construction as well as bad electronics.  However I tried this unit, and I must say I was quite pleased.  Yes it is not extremely solid in construction, yet is quite light on the head which is important if you’re gonna keep it on most of the day.  The headphones are indeed stereo, and I have learned to enjoy the intimacy of music and other computer audio.  Most important however is that the microphone is quite sensitive, and I realized that the speech recognition software is not as bad as I thought, it was just the quality of the microphone I was using before was not picking up my voice correctly.  However this microphone, which is easily adjustable, does a great job of picking up the voice, and I find a 90% reduction in mistaken text from my dictation.  In fact, this review is being "dictated" using this unit! For the price this is really a great unit.  Of course if one is looking for sound with a booming bass, then I suggest buying specific headphones for that purpose.  This is fine for me however and the reason for the purchase really has to do with the voice recognition, which it does perfectly.  Its software downloads to your computer easily with the USB port (and a very generous cable length),and the interface between the headphones, the computer, and either Window's built-in speech recognition software, or any other software you may purchase is carefree.  It is truly “plugged and go”! No need to look any further for these needs than this Koss Headset-Microphone..

title: Very good sound quality, great comfort
text:
These earbuds were up against some tough competition. I regularly use my Airpods with my apple products (which "just work," but are not super comfortable) and my Jabra's (which are outstanding in every way, but were triple the price of the Soul S-Nano's, so it's not really fair...)

So keeping in mind the affordability of the Soul S-Nano buds, I was really impressed.

Sound quality:

My test album for audio stuff is deadmou5 - "here's the drop!"
- Bass 3/5 - You definitely hear the lows, but you won't feel them in your teeth
- 3D sound 5/5 - Really good. I ended up closing my eyes for a couple tracks and "watching" the music in that way you can when you can hear it coming from different "parts of the room" on a good 3D track.
- Clarity 4.5/5 - For buds? This small? Pretty darn good. Instrumentals were clear, treble sounds great and beats are crisp.
- Volume - subjective. I'll say these can get painfully loud. Be careful!
- hear-through feature - I don't use it. I don't use it on my Jabra's either. It's just sounded weird to me on whatever buds I've used it on and I've never liked it. It does work. It actually sounds better on the Soul buds that it does on my Jabra's, but it's a personal preference thing.

Comfort:

- 5/5. I have princess ears. I find earpod/airpods pretty uncomfortable I usually prefer over-the-ear cans for comfort. These buds are VERY comfortable. They come with three sets of tips, so you can pick the ones that fit best for you. They stay in my ears without being "suction-y" and I can wear them for hours.

Controls/connection:

- Touch controls 4/5 - These take some getting used to. Read the quick-start guide to learn the gestures (there are more than I thought and some are not intuitive). Generally, they're pretty reliable, but sometimes the pause doesn't stay paused and volume control goes up instead of down because it doesn't pick up both taps. It's also very easy to accidentally set off a control just doing normal stuff. I'm afraid I'm going to accidentally call someone taking out an earbud or something.
- Bluetooth stability 4/5 - Once connected, the buds usually remember the connection. Sometimes they don't automatically reconnect; sometimes they do. Overall, this has been pretty good and even when it doesn't work, it's very easy to fix manually by reconnecting to your phone using the phone settings menu.
- Initial connection 5/5 - Very easy. No problems at all connecting!

Battery/case:

Battery life 5/5 - I've been using these for a couple days and am listening to them right now. I've been working and jamming out for two hours and I'm only down to 80% battery. And then I can put them in the case and top up.
Case 3/5 - This was the only real disappointment for me. The case does not seem super durable to me. The plastic is thin enough that you can see the LEDs on the buds through the case. Seeing as you need the case to charge the buds, if the case breaks, you're out of luck. I've cut up a vinyl sticker to put on the case for just a little extra protection, but I'm still a little wary of just throwing it into my bag or leaving it hanging on my purse strap where it can get bumped into and cracked. Compared to the Jabra and Airpod cases, it is very flimsy.
Charging 5/5 - the case charges fast and has a USB-C connection. Not a micro-usb port in sight. The included cable is VERY short, though, so if that doesn't work for you, grab another one that you have at home. It will work fine.

So overall... 4.5 out of 5. For the price, these buds are quite good!

title: Not quite as good as the Bose QC35
text:
These are perfectly good headphones, but since they're a copycat product they have to be judged in comparison to the product they're copying (Bose QC35).

-Noise cancelling - Winner Sony. The Bose are really good but I think the Sony's are noticeably better.
- Sound quality - tie - both are very good
- Bluetooth range - Winner Sony - The Sony's have a slightly more stable connection in worst-case conditions (when running a microwave nearby which is across the house from the Bluetooth connection, the Bose drop out more than the Sony's do.)
- Connectivity - Winner Bose - The Bose can connect to 2 devices, they honestly don't work super well (sometimes it's not clear which ones are connected or there's some bugginess). But at least Bose is trying - Sony's only connect to one device... to switch devices you have to turn off the bluetooth on the device and manually connect to the other device which is a PITA.
- Interface - Winner Bose - Lot of minor stuff. Bose has really good voice synthesis, and can pronounce your computer name. For example, I named my computer "The Mattbook Pro", and the Bose successfully pronounces it: "Connected to... the Mattbook pro". Obviously the voice isn't preprogrammed, and it's voice synthesis is surprisingly good. The Sony is okay but it just has per-recorded voice clips so it can't say the name of the device it's connected to. Next, the play/pause on the Sony is okay, and I think the touchpad gestures are pretty good/logical. But they're inconsistent, sometimes the play/pause double tap doesn't register, sometimes the track forward gesture registers as volume down, etc., etc. The discrete buttons on the Bose are better, although they're not perfect either, there's double tapping, triple tapping, etc, to control track fw/back, which are annoying to execute.
- Comfort - Winner Bose - The Bose earcups are a little comfier in my opinion.
- Appearance - Winner Bose - The Sony's are unnecessarily large, I think the Bose look a little nicer. The Sony's stick out farther than necessary.
- Charging - Winner Sony - The Sony charges via USB-C which is nicer and more future-proof than micro USB the Bose uses. But it's not that big of a deal.

Anyway, I was originally skeptical of bluetooth headsets due to their price, but if you don't have a pair I'd highly recommend buying a pair. Both the Sony's and the Bose ones are pretty good, so just get whichever one you like the best.

text:
I currently have a Sony DR-BT22, a MDR-A30 and a MDR-W24. I also had a countless number of Sony headphones and earphones from the good old days. The Sony's from the good old days sounded really great.

I try to find one that is as good as any of the Sony. This Koss KPH14W is not it.

The spec printed on the box is as follows.
3.5 mm plug
4 feet long cord
100 - 15,000 Hz
18 Ohms
104 dB SPL

This Koss sounds average at best. I think the best I can describe the differences is that the Sony's sound like an expensive 2.1 speaker system with clean sound and house-shaking bass. The Koss is just a very average 2.0 speaker system. It is not FM/AM radio bad. It is just average. Your car radio sounds better.

The fit of the Koss is very bad. It is for kid with small head. The Koss is at least an inch shorter than the Sony. The plastic material is hard plastic. It clamps to my head and inside my ears so tight. It hurts. Compared the plastic from the Sony, the Sony uses soft flexible rubbery plastic. The Sony is soft like a pillow but very supportive at the same time.

I have to follow the advice from the other reviewers. I use my hair dryer to soften the plastic. So, I can bent it wider. Even it is wider, it is still too short and not comfortable.

On the positive side, the Koss has the longest cord. It is 4 feet long. The plug is in a 140 degree angle.

I have some pictures. The white one is the Koss. The picture with the Koss inside the packaging is how tight it is. It is a clamp. You can see how wide I have to bent it to fit better.

I cannot recommend this Koss. It is too small for an adult and the sound is just average.

title: Loved these, but I'm incredibly unlucky
text:
These were great, honestly. I got the package when expected, and they worked great. The sound is pretty good and they don't leak that much at all. The headphones are not heavy or anything, and sit pretty comfortably on your head. I buy headphones all the time (I have about 7 pairs), and I definitely liked these out of all the wireless ones I've owned. I also got a ton of compliments on these, because they look super cool. The blue light might be annoying for those who don't want their headphones flashing, but it didn't bother me at all.

Now here's the sad part. I was wearing these outside about a month after I got them (so this was in like late March or early April), and out of nowhere, it was pouring snow. That's right. SNOW. I didn't even know that snow could so that, but Michigan weather, ya know? Sunny one day and then a blizzard the next. Anyway, I rushed under cover and pulled off these headphones to stuff them in my backpack but they were soaked (and I really wasn't outside for much longer after the snow started. That's what I mean when I say that it was pouring snow). A bit after that incident, I noticed that the bluetooth isn't really the same, and that there's this static that happens when I use them. They only work well when I use the cord that came with them.

*sigh* These were great, but Michigan weather is a bitch. I'll be ordering these again, and this time I'll be a little more careful.

title: A decade with the ER4S
text:
My pair of ER4S is about to turn 10 years old. I thought enough time had passed to finally write an Amazon review. Heh heh. I was the second person on Headwize.com (before there was a Head-Fi) to get them and post comments. I've used a seemingly endless number of headphones over the years: Sennheiser HD580, Denon 950, Sony 7509, Sony 7506, Sony MDR600, Koss ESP950 electrostatics, about half a dozen Koss dynamic headphones, one pair of Stax, Ixos' top of the line 1001, Pioneer's top of the line DJing headphones, two models of AKG studio headphones, JVC's former top of the line (only available direct), HN-7506, both versions of the Extreme Isolation UR-29, and a seemingly unending number of cheapos bundled with music players.

Whew! So what do I think about the Etymotic Research ER4S? I think it is frankly without peer amongst those cans I've heard. It is flat, transparent, resolved, extended, dynamic, fast, tight, totally grain-free, and impossible to distort. It is not capable of the inner-light of, say, Pierre Gabriel of Quebec's loudspeaker systems, or the sheer delicacy, finesse, and seeming perfection of Burmeister of Germany's loudspeakers. But those are, after all, loudspeakers. I've never heard any headphones achieve what those two audiophile names have. And yes, I have listened to them thoroughly and been marveled. If you question my ears, I was the only person in a room run by Thiele at CES (filled with audiophiles and magazine writers) to point out repeatedly and correctly when the active cabling technology was changed without us seeing.

People all have different tastes. We all have different hearing responses, even if slight. Our ear canals vary. And on and on. Your results may vary. But when I can take some of the most lauded DJ mixers and compare them adequately using such a relatively inexpensive piece of gear when heretofore it was only possible to do such comparisons on large nightclub sound systems, I feel pretty confident the little Etys are doing enough right to recommend them. Over time, I have found the black foam earpieces to give the best sound and comfort, but the white rubber flanged tips certainly isolate better, which if there's background noise is more beneficial to the sound than anything else. Years ago, I preferred the sound of the flange tips. Maybe I have hearing loss? Maybe I just didn't test the foam ones enough? Don't know, but they come with both, so you have no excuse not to try both. You can also get larger yellow foam ones and smaller blue flanged rubber tips. I tried the blues recently and they were too small to seal properly.

A word of advice on the flanged tips, use a dab of water on them, pull your ear up slightly, and put it in so the edge of the flanges are the same depth on both ears. After a few minutes, assuming you don't have ear problems, the pressure of the air between the earphone and the eardrum will equalize since the tympanic membrane is slowly permeable to air. If there's not much bass, you don't have it in deep enough, you need a better headphone jack, or the source device sucks. Most MP3 players have poor headphone jacks, so don't blame the Ety for having an impedance of 100ohms and wanting a touch more of current capability. In spite of that, they still sound impressive connected even to cheap gear. I have a $40 portable CD player with a monster headphone jack that, combined with the Ety, you'd have to pay a significant sum to keep me from using on airline flights. It makes flying not only tolerable, but something to look forward to.

title: Great headphones. Expensive.
text:
These headphones are fantastic. I guess I took a star off because for the money, these should be perfect, and there are just a few small issues.

Pros:
-Fantastic sound These give very clear, bright, life-like sound, (This may be a problem for those of you who want deep bass, as some is lost, or at least not amplified as it is in Beats by Dre, and that type of bud).
-Great fit, great options for ear tips.
-Narrow diameter driver channel is less painful after long use compared to wider channel ear buds

Cons:
-Stick straight out of the ear canals - can't sleep in them or wear under a beanie, and any pull on the cables really torques in your ears!
-Picks up wind - the braided cable and the part of the bud sticking from the ear both pick up wind noise. Not for riding on your bike!
-Expensive

Overall, though, they are fantastic. The sound is almost unparalleled. If the shape of the ear bud is not to you liking, I would recommend the Shure E315. Similar in terms of comfort, quality of sound, and variety of ear tips, but the cables go up and over your ear, reducing some of the issues with wind and fit. But overall, I would call it a draw between the two.

title: Great earbuds, but not all purpose
text:
I love my ER4Ps but they aren't for everything.

The sound is great, and I love the noise canceling. If it was just this then I'd give it the maximum number of stars.

Issues:
I only wear ear buds to work out, so when anything taps the cord it acts like a microphone sending noise to the bud.

They do not stand up to constant working out. I've been through 2 sets already, each one lasted about 2 years before a wire disconnects from the green barrel (both failed in exact same spot). When the 1st set broke I sent it in to be repaired, which cost right about what a brand new pair would cost. I'm pretty sure they didn't even bother repairing it and just sent me a new pair. When the 2nd set broke I tried to take the barrel apart to reconnect them which was a terrible idea :).

Summary:
sitting still -- effing awesome.
running -- lots of *thump* *thump* *thump* from the cord bouncing on your chest.
sound -- superb.
durability -- not so much.

The higher end of the audio products.

title: I Took the Pepsi Challenge
text:
Pulp Fiction Metaphorical Comparison...

LANCE (to Vincent):

"...Now this is Panda [ER-6], from Mexico. Very good stuff. This is Bava [ER-6i], different, but equally good. And this is Choco [ER-4P] from the Hartz Mountains of Germany....but this one...(pointing to the Choco)...this one's a little more expensive...But when you shoot it, you'll know where that extra money went..."

IMHO, the same can be said about the ER4P's: You'll know where the extra money went. Spending the extra $$$ is well worth it. Yes, I've purchased all three (for my iPod) and settled on the BBME (biggest-best-most EXPENSIVE). My hunt for a fantastic IE set has finally come to an end. Keep in mind, before experimenting with the Etymotic series, I've previously owned Sony's (MDR-EX71SL & MDR-EX81SL) and onto Sennheiser (CX300's). If you're on a budget and like lots of bass, the CX300 top both Sony models.

As far as the Etymotic are concerned, my first purchase was the ER-6. While I'm sure with a proper fit and amplification, they are great. However, with my iPod, and a poor fit with the flanges, and mediocre fit with the foam, I gave up. Because of a poor fit, they sounded like faint tin cans. PROPER fit is a MUST for any IE headphone to function correctly.

Manufactured specifically for small media players, I tried the ER6i. The triple flange when wet, fit snugly and sealed well. It is important to follow the directions to acheive a proper fit. There was a huge difference in sound over the previous. After listening to them for two days, I tried my old CX300's on and found out how artifical the bass was, and how they muddied the sound. The same cannot be said for the ER6i's. While I found the bass to be lighter, I didn't mind, and managed my EQ to adjust (R & B worked best). I've read complaints about the bass, especially when listening to rap. I don't agree. I found it very satisfactory. The ER6i's are worth the money if you cannot afford the Choco...

At twice the price of the ER6i's the ER-4P's better offer something special-and they do! Extra accessories aside, the sound was unmatched by the above. I tested both without any EQ at the same volume level. While the ER6i's were a little more punchy in the bass and had a warmer overall tone, the ER4P's walked all over them as far as a realistic presentation of the music. What did I find? Clarity, near flawless sound & tonality, and just enough bass to keep me happy. An EQ adjustment back to R & B brought up the bass a little, and took a little of the edge off the high end.

To conclude, if you're willing to shell out the big bucks, then go for the ER-4's. However, the ER-6i's are well worth the price ($10-$20 more than the CX300's), especially if you're on a budget. Either way, you can't go wrong, but for me, I'll stick with the Choco.

title: 10 year Etymotic user
text:
I got my first ER4S set 10 years ago and a second set a couple of years later to ensure that I would not be without some Etymotics. Both sets are fine after all this time and use but I want a 3rd set, but the next will be the ER-4P!

IMO, the single best thing about the ER4S is their durability. I've literally owned dozens of earphone sets and all but the Etymotics that I continued to use eventually bit the dust. Usually it was a cord discontinuity most likely very near the plug. I've replaced countless cables and plugs, pulling out my soldering iron and rummaging through my collection of parts. Once I got the Etymotics I had put all that behind me. Not once have I had a problem with the ER4S cables or plugs. The only times I have experienced cutout of a channel was when a filter got clogged, which has happened a few times. It's pretty simple to replace a filter, and they give you extra filters and a tool to remove the old filter. I figure I can probably clean the old filters but haven't bothered trying because I have an ample supply of new ones.

I bought the Etymotics because I needed some privacy at my new office job. It wasn't just that I wanted my space, I had a lot of thinking to do and needed to block out distracting noise and at times there was far too much of that. I did some research and determined that the Etymotics were a likely good choice. They were highly touted by audiophiles and had a reputation for being very effective in noisy environments. Of course, they still enjoy that reputation. I no longer have that office job and I mostly use the Etymotics in the gym, where their isolation is just as critical as at that office job.

When I read the reviews before buying my first ER4S I quickly realized that people who used them with portable devices seemed to always use headphone amps, and I assumed that I too would need one and so I bought an Airhead "Headphone Amplifier and Audio Image Processor" at the same time. However, to my amazement and delight I found that I got adequate volume from my portable devices without having to use it. I did use the amp when listening to audio files at my computer, at least sometimes, but have ever since just set aside the Airhead. I have used the ER4S phones without an amplifier with satisfactory results with a Sony WM-FX465 cassette/TV/FM/AM portable, iRiver SlimX IMP-350 portables, iRiver H120 and H140 portables and Sansa Sandisk M250 MP3/FM portables (2 different firmware/chipset models).

My hearing isn't the best, and I won't get into subtle discussions concerning performance in various frequency ranges. However, I recently acquired a set of Sennheiser CX300B earbud headphones and determined that the Etymotics sound far superior. I also don't expect that the Sennheisers are very durable. Also, they came with only one set of buds that fit my ears. The Etymotics came with several sets of both types of buds (the white plastic, which I always use and the foam). I bought extra white plastic tips, but have only had to replace a couple (they got a bit loose over time and would remain in my ear after pulling out the drivers).

It is true that the sound from brushing the cable goes right to your ears and it's a major annoyance. I rarely notice that now, having developed strategies to avoid brushing the cables. I'll take the durability over other considerations!

Lately, I use the ER4S with small Sandisk MP3 players, the M250's. There are 4 different types of M250's and 2 of mine aren't as loud as the 3rd at maximum volume and I've had problems achieving satisfactory listening levels with them at times when using the ER4S's so I anticipate getting the more efficient ER-4P for my 3rd set of Etymotics at some point. I've been reading reviews and considered getting another brand, but I think I'd probably regret that and plan to stick with Etymotic. Fortunately, the price has come down from the $269 + shipping I paid for my last set!

title: Real Review - Quantified by Examples & Comparisons...
text:
If you are like me, you are struggling through the various reviews to divine what the review considers great sound and how these compare to the real world (versus a recording engineer loving their URI's all mid-range.) In most cars, I would configure the audio system (on a -5 to +5 system) Treble +5, Mid 0 to -5, and Bass +5. I believe at low volume, a system should give you the dynamics of sitting in front of an orchestra, not just acoustic guitar and voice. I use a 5th Generation iPod, and with these ear phones, the LOUDNESS EQ setting. (My past phones on this unit: Original, Bose in-ear, Tri-Ports & Quiet Comfort2.) I like (and have) pretty much all music but country, opera and gangsta.

Addressing the concerns I had when reading the reviews:

Bass.

Yes, these do not compare to Bose's in-ear and tri-ports for booming bass. However, the treble response and crispness do rival the Bose . First you must carefully follow insertion instructions. Then, the Bass is there, however it is very, very accurate and tight. It also requires some volume to bring it out. Throw on some Techmaster PEB and it will render the speaker blowing sub-bass perfectly (this killed my original iPod units.) Have the volume below 50% on Lady Gaga / Beyonce's Telephone, and you will not hear any bass presence. 75% volume and you hear the bass, perfectly and as it was meant to be heard.

In fact, below 50% volume on anything and you do not really hear the bass. This is also because the treble and mid-range performance is amazing and drowns it out. If you are like me and do not like a lot of Mid-Range, you must use the LOUDNESS EQ setting, or the mid-range can bring a headache on.

Volume.

The P versions do not suffer the power issues Bose QC2's do, and better the Tri-Ports and in-ears for ability to pump volume cleanly. You can almost max out every song and feel like you're in a South Beach club with you head next to an amp with an iPod's power. The sweet spot is 60% to 90%. I could also spot the iTunes Plus songs I bought versus the CD's I ripped by compression issues of the iTunes music. These things have a clarity that is truly amazing.

Comfort & Fit.

They fit well when you follow the instructions, but they take a bit to get out of your ears, and it can hurt if you rush it. While I like to throw them on while brushing my teeth in the morning, these are not quick on quick off things. You must remove one side to take a phone call, they do block. Also, like any ear plug, they feel a bit unnatural to me, and the absence of ambient noise feels strange. The "rustling" of the cables has not bothered me much yet, but they do make it thump, so I guess if you jog with them it might get irritating. PS: No matter how clean you think your ears are, have a napkin ready when you take these out.

Conclusion:

I do not know about the wire's longevity (my last Bose In-Ears died from cable failure) and that is my biggest concern. However, I do think they are better than the Bose offerings, the price and discomfort of them being paid back and then some in clarity and accuracy of sound. Really, you will not believe an iPod is capable of this quality.

title: Accurate monitors for sure.  Highly Recommend.
text:
Hello all, I purchased a set of Etymotic ER-4Ps around a month ago. ( September 2009 ) I have listened to a wide variety of music from a few different sources. Primary music focus for very critical listening: Movie scores/Classical/Jazz/Psy-Trance. Sources include PC/Laptop/iPhone/Amplifier.

These in ear monitors allow a lot of details to come through. They do a nice job of isolating ambient noise. They will also let you hear every single tick and crackle in a cheap PC integrated sound card. On a nicer PC sound card or real amplifier they sound great. They are efficient enough to play very well from an iPhone. ( I need to use an adapter as they will not fit direct to first gen iPhone )

I have listened to the James Horner score to Sneakers countless times since the score was released. I know its details better than any other album. It is my own reference point. In my home stereo setup when I upgraded my speakers to some Cambridge Soundworks T200 full towers. I was so amazed at the details I never heard before. Shocked in fact that I have never made them out before. The same level of shock was realized with the ER-4Ps. I am hearing yet again, more details I have never ever noticed before on the Sneakers soundtrack. Specifically an upright bass recorded at very low levels in the background of several tracks. They are deep in the background and until I heard the score on the ER-4Ps I never it was there in as many places as it is. This experience is repeating with many albums. I am going through all my favorite albums anticipating hearing things I always missed. That is exciting. For that reason alone I recommend these highly.

The point is these IEMs ( In Ear Monitors ) play what you give them. They do not mask, enhance or change the sound at all. I used a freeware utility ( sinegen.exe ) to do some tone generator tests. The ER-4Ps trail off rapidly between 16.5khz and 17 khz. This is really not going to be noticeable in a track. I am comparing to a 15 year old pair of Denon Over the Ear-phones who have served me well up to this point. The Denons ( on the same source PC ) trailed off very gradually but audio could be heard to about 22k with volume levels set way up. The ER-4Ps trail off to 0 by 17.5-18k regardless of amplification levels. Again let me be clear that I am hearing clarity and definition much greater in the ER-4Ps than the Denons.

Working my way through the sound level spectrum output is consistent and linear, read: very flat, way far down. You can hear a sine wave generation down to 25 hz. Levels trail off to 0 below that. It seems that the correct levels of energy are reproduced through a very wide range.

Let me be clear, the CORRECT level is produced. These do not over-boom-ify like most in ear cannons are expected to do to provide brain massages. IF there is heavy bass recorded, you WILL hear it. If the recording was made ( often ) to anticipate a system with the bass turned up to eleventy-seven, you will not hear much deep bass.

You will hear the music, as it is recorded. They are clearly monitors. They may not be for everyone who wants purely entertainment in a casual environment. If you appreciate accuracy and fidelity and expect to hear so many details of a track, these ARE the IEMs for you.

They do a very nice job of muting outside noise. I have been able to wrap the cords over my ears, forward then over and around the back to all but eliminate the microphone effect. The clip provided also helps with that. Without wrapping or clipping the cables will pick up a lot of noise. Ambient in-the-air noise is cut way down.

In the office I work in, there is steady hum of air conditioning , the lite-fm over the PA, and in the computer data center, deafening cooling and equipment noise. Wearing these nulls out those sounds very well. Better than foam insert ear plugs, with no audio even playing. With a track playing you are in your own sonic universe. Really amazing.

They are great in a library too. You can have them on at standard listening levels and the person sitting next to you will not hear them. The apple ear buds waste so much sound ( and people play them so loud ) that I can usually make out words from 20 foot away from some listeners. It bothers me, and it must indicate severe hearing damage to the poor listener. Not a problem with the ER-4Ps. You and you alone hear all the music and only the music through the ER-4Ps.

You do not need to play these loud at all to hear everything. They handle high volumes nicely tho. Be careful tho, you could will likely do damage to your ears turning these up to full power.

The ER-4Ps take a few seconds each ear to seat correctly. I have not had the troubles that others have had. My ears happen to fit fine with the standard smaller mushroom cap inserts. You will know you have a good fit when outside noise drops to about 5% normal. I gave them 4 stars for comfort because after an hour or so it feels like its time to take them out and let your ears breath and stretch a bit. That may be the case with all in-ears.

I got a chance to listen to some V-Modas that my cousin got last year. They were 1/2 the price as the ER-4Ps. They were not as accurate, but definitely more "fun". I would recommend V-Modas ( not sure the model but they go for around $80) for casual listeners who want big booms. They are a bit easier to insert and take out.

I waited over a month to write a review. I did not want to give a pre-mature/just-spent-the-cash-and-now-I-must-justify-it/fan-boy review.

Edit: One possible downside, the cabling is very fine. I am very careful with them always. It feels like you *need* to be careful with them. For transport the kit does come with a larger hard case and small soft zipper pouch. The low mass of the earpiece and cabling makes them effectively weightless in your ears.

I am truly enjoying them. And listening to them for a few hours a day at work without fatigue.

Update: July 2010.
I still love them! They are holding up perfectly, sound great, and I would still recommend them.

Update: December 2015
Still using them basically every day at work. Good stuff.
Their accuracy will expose weaknesses in your source. These sounded amazing on the LG G2. But kinda meh on the LG G4. Looking into an external DAC/Amp.

Update: January 2016
Oh noes! I just had my first indication of the cabling finally letting go. One channel is dropping out depending on how the cable is moved. Replacement cables are available from $35 to $200+. When I replace the cables it will be of the cheaper variety. I might attempt to replace the bad portion of the cable and DIY a patch.

Daniel

title: Best Bang For Your Buck
text:
Of all of the headphones I've used to date, I've found that these ones definitely offer the most "bang for your buck!" I highly recommend them. In fact, I can't recommend them enough. I'm on my third pair, and I've consistently experienced the same quality from each.

Here are the short, sweet points:

1) Ninety percent of the time, I use mine for running and biking with my iPhone/iPod. I sweat obnoxiously, and they still hold up against the "moisture" (which is an understatement). They're definitely durable. If you're that athlete hunting for "the pair", these are a solid bet to go with!

2) They really don't kid about the "ultra lightweight" aspect! These are amazingly lightweight and flexible, and that lends to an amazing fit. They don't hurt my ears (or head) from pushing or squeezing too firmly.

3) The sound quality is great for my standards. These compare (or surpass) any I've used.

4) The only (minor) issue I experience is that if they ever come out of my ears for a moment (i.e. I bump them or take them out to say "hey" to someone), sweat can get into my ear, and they sometimes run into issues. It's rare, and the results are typically minor, but it can create that "underwater" effect, reducing the volume and quality slightly. Usually, a simple re-shift or drying out of my ear will alleviate the problem.

5) If was being really picky, I'd say they could also benefit from a cord management system (e.g. a free clip). However, relative to others, they have a pretty ideal cord length (i.e. as little excess as seems possible).

If you've read this far and want my typical "wordier" review, read on for my follow-up points:

1) Sweat/Life: Like anything, they're not invincible. They don't even claim to be waterproof, so more power to them! Typically after five to six months of using each pair daily, they eventually bite the dust. That's from one to two hour workouts, constantly being chucked in and out of a gym bag, and surviving whatever other wears come their way. Toward the end of their life, I'll eventually begin to experience an occasional short-out in one of the speakers during the "peak" of my workout (a.ka. the part where I sweat nastiest). However, they'll dry out by the next day and be good to go. After about another month of this routine, they'll become unusable. From my experience, that's a great lifespan- especially for the price you can find these at.

2) Fit: They sit so gently set in my ear canals, yet they stay in so well. I've never had them come off unless I accidentally knock them off. Honestly, I've sort of "forgotten" I have them in at times. Because I don't think about them, I've gone to scratch my head or wipe sweat, and I've dumbly knocked them lose. They're design blows my mind. It's just so ideal. I've even gone through a number of hair-dos (ranging from longer to completely buzzed), and they still stay on just as well. They're very adjustable because of a precise range of ratcheted positions.

3) Sound Quality: I can't say I've owned "premium sound" sound sport headphones, so this is always the toughest part for me to review. I like to think that I know good sound and appreciate high quality. Based on that alone, I say these are great. I pump songs with heavy bass (i.e. budstep, rock, etc...), and they sound great to me. More "objectively", I can at least compare them to other things like my premium car audio, Apple Earbuds, and so forth. Based on all of that, they sound just as good to me.

4) Sweat (Part 2): I don't have much extra to say here. Basically, this is rarely an issue, but it's a point worth noting. Because they're not water proof, they don't have any special seals. I just make a habit of not taking them out until I'm done, and everything is usually fine. I just pause my music if I need to stop and hear something. And that's not to say I can't ever take them out. I've done so many times without any problem. It's just a rule I've made to avoid even risking it.

5) Cord Management: I rarely notice this problem. I generally just let them hang and don't run into issues. Because of they're great fit, I can easily throw the cord behind me or wear it down the front- depending on how I'm working out. On rare occasions, I use a clip from an old pair of headphones, and that helps a lot. Personally, I just hate dealing with clips, so it's almost not even worth the extra effort.

It might be important to note that I have used several various headphones over the years, and these are what I ended up on. To give you some comparison, I have tried various Apple "Earbuds" (i.e. [[ASIN:B004DEPOA0 Apple Earphones with Remote and Mic (NEWEST VERSION)[Retail Packaging]]]), Griffin TuneBuds (i.e. [[ASIN:B0015ADWMW Griffin TuneBuds Mobile for iPhone 3G, 3GS (Black)]]), and even nicer Sennheiser sport sets (i.e. [[ASIN:B001GT185K Sennheiser PMX80 In-Ear Sport Series II Behind the Head Earphones]]).

text:
I wanted so badly to like this, but I just can't. First off, if you have a sleeping partner, this things has a blinking light the entire time it's in operation. FIne for you because you can't see it, but your partner won't appreciate it very much. Strike one. So I tried it on and after figuring out I could slide the earbuds along the cloth channel, tried to lay down. The earbuds are not low-profile enough and dug into the side of my head, but it wasn't too bad so I thought "meh, I can live with that."

It turns out, I couldn't live with that. This is because there is no earthly way to adjust the mask to where it's covering my eyes and the earbuds are covering my ears at the same time. It may be my head shape or it may be a design flaw, but I could NOT comfortably position the earbuds to cover my ears without having to push the eyemask either up off my eyes or down below. As my ears are pretty much normally aligned with my eyes (I took drawing classes--I know the proper alignment and ratio, LOL), I would say it's some sort of design flaw. And the earbuds are still uncomfortable to lie on. Strike two.

But the coupe de grâce, or the straw that broke the camel's back was the fact that, as others have mentioned, a voice comes on unexpectedly to yell "Connected!!!!" at highly inopportune times--multiple times. A very bad feature for something purported to help you sleep.

I'm just lying there, about to drift off, and "CONNECTED!" Whaaaa??? I *was* connected, thankyouverymuch. Now I'm awake and angry. Strike three, you're going back.

title: Finally - They stay on my ears and sound good
text:
I have had way too many sets of headphones. Mostly because my dog eats them if they are within reach. While I still have not found the perfect headset with these, they come pretty close.

Durability and battery Life - Way too early to tell. I'll update this after a few months.

Noise Canceling- Let’s get something straight - if you put your fingers in your ears, they will cancel noise. That's called passive noise canceling, or simply, blocking outside noise. True active noise canceling head phones are over the ear, and usually very expensive. These head phones do a pretty good job passively blocking outside noise by fitting very well to the ear and being angled correctly.

Sound - Everyone has different tastes when it comes to what they like to hear. Some headphones have good or bad ranges from high to low. But it is the quality of the range that matters. For instance, I like to hear bass, and to me there is nothing worse than a tinny am radio sound. These definitely have bass, but it's a bit muddy. The good news is I was able to adjust the equalizer on my phone to clean it up, mostly. Overall all though, for the price, the sound quality is pretty darn good.

Fit & Hold - They Fit and stay put! The best part of these headphones is they fit my ears perfectly. The part that goes around the ear has a wire going through it, unlike so many others. This allows you to mold the over ear wires exactly to you ear and they do not fall out. None of the last several sets I had do this, and it is an enormous benefit.

Controls - The are typical up and down volume and a center button that is used for on, off, hold, answer, etc. I wish the volume buttons were reversed, but that's just being picky. They announce power on, power off and connected. Sadly, they do not announce battery life.

Appearance – Meh. They are a bit big and boxy, but I don’t know how that‘s different from having white things hanging out of your ears for $200.00

Overall - I am giving this 5 starts not because they are the best headphones. I am giving them 5 starts because they check off almost all of my boxes and the price it great. So, 5 stars for overall function and price.

Note: I paid full price for these and I was not asked to review them. Also, if you like this review, please indicate so below. Thanks.

title: Happy with this choice
text:
These sound great. I don't have golden ears, but I believe I can at least partly tell the difference between good and bad headphones/earbud. I loved my last pair, sony buds that I only replaced because the cord finally gave in after probably 6 or 7 years.

The complaints about putting these in are founded, but honestly, if you spend a little time practising, it's not complicated and you can find easier ways. Sometimes I'll put the cord over the ear first, then fold the bud into the canal. Other time, the opposite. I tug on my lobe with the thumb and ring finger and use my index finger to apply pressure on the body of the plug to seat it in my canal.

I do run with these in. They block a lot of sound, but not everything. I' pretty hyper vigilant about my surrounding when I'm running, so I'm usually very aware anyway. I wear them to listen to music while working in the workshop and it turned the quite loud combination of my radial arm saw + shop vac into an EXTREMELY manageable background sound, and I could still hear my son yell at me to shut it off when he wanted to ride his bike in the garage - all without taking away too much from the music.

In less than perfect settings, like resting my head against a pillow (or car seat) they do start to hurt a bit after about an hour. General wear, however, hasn't really had that effect.

The cord doesn't tangle remotely as much as my previous pair, but I hope to keep up the habit of winding them and putting them in the pouch that comes with them.
I got the "black", but they are transparent black. I'd rather opaque, but really, it's not a big deal.
I do sometimes wish the distance between the "Y" where the L/R cords connect was a little longer, again, it's not bothered me enough to dock points, really.
I'd actually give a 4.5/5 but don't feel the need to take away an entire star.

(Update)
7 months it made it without a hitch. Then the right side started to flake on me. I have to contort the wire and get lucky to get sound, which usually stays fine until I remove them and have to do it again the nest time I use them. I'll be returning to Shure for a replacement, but I have to say that my previous Sony pair, with near daily use, lasted 6-7 YEARS without issue, so this bothers me. I'm certain Shure will replace at least the cable, otherwise I'd be dropping more than the one star I took off. I'll update if I have other issues with the replacement process or otherwise.

title: Beautifully designed product with good noise cancellation
text:
Unboxing: Wouldn't usually make a section of this, but every once in a while a product makes it a pleasure. Especially a weird one like this. It's like unboxing a little UFO. It starts out in something like a hat box with a couple sticky tabs of tape to remove. Wish they could have found a better closure method, but the box is nice. Inside that you're immediately presented with the odd looking earbuds and a starter guide (also round) that has you immediately trying them on and fitting the best sleeve size for in your ear. There are no extra sleeves obviously apparent, so time to dig deeper. Next up is the UFO. A large earbud like this needs a large charging case. This one is round and unzips like some of the nicer headphone cases, but it's also a hard case with lights and buttons. Nothing inside but a charging dock. Under it is a secret compartment (made less secret by the thumb holes for easy removal). At the bottom of the hat box we have our missing sleeves and a charging cord.

Even with a diagram, putting these on was confusing and took four tries. Once they're on though, they are quite comfortable, and I think I'll learn to put them on after a few more tries.

Back to the book, and ugh! now they're telling me to put them in the charging case to pair. But I just finally got them on! &*^@#!

Ok, after getting things paired and back on, I'm able to put them through some testing. I'm not really an audiophile, but I've tried a lot of earbuds. Comfort is good. They don't rely on being stuck in your ear to hold themselves up, so there isn't a high stress point that's going to get sore first. They sound good. Better than most, but not the best I've heard. The control button is on the back of your ear, and I find it awkward and unreliable. Noise cancellation is solid, but like every other one I've tried, it is hard to tell sometimes because it scales with volume. Turning them on in a noisy room doesn't result in a quiet room, but turning up what you are listening to will result in noise other than what you are listening to disappearing quite a lot. There is a passthrough mode if you need to hear what's going on around you, but it doesn't sound very nice.

I like that it's USB-C. No more having to turn the cord over three times to figure out which end is up, and much faster charging. The case has three lights to show you charge progress for the case Each one represents enough charge for one full use of the earbuds. There's also a light on the top to tell you whether the earbuds are charged yet.

It's a solid product. Not my top favorite, but definitely innovative and a competitive offering.

title: Good Experience...But Only After Upgrades
text:
This is my second pair of IEMs, and I bought them as more of a backup. I'd read about these having a high value-to-price ratio and being very comfortable, so I went in with extremely high expectations.

Unfortunately my first impressions of these were that they were awful. As compared with my other pair (an older model from Ultimate Ears) I found it to be incredibly difficult to get a proper seal. The sound felt tinny and washed out. And comfort? Quite the opposite: Pain.

I almost gave up, re-packed them, and send them back. But I decided to invest further. I bought a set of Comply tips and tried those instead of the stock tips. HUGE upgrade! I was able to get a great seal and the comfort level shot way up. But Comply tips aren't cheap; the set of 3 pairs costs more than 20% of what I paid for these IEMs, so I'm removing one star there.

Comfort was still not where I wanted it and eventually I realized that the problem was the absolute piece of garbage cable that these came with. It's stiff, plasticy feeling, doesn't fall naturally, and I was constantly fighting with the memory wire. I upgraded to a much better cable--another 30% cost boost (second star deduction)--and now I had one of the two things I'd originally come for: A very comfortable setup.

So, now that I have comfort and seal, how about the sound? Impressive, actually, even at the 50% price bump point to which I'd taken things. I listen to electronic music primarily, so I like plenty of bass. These certainly deliver there. Very decent clarity on the high end as well. Sound doesn't sparkle nearly as much as it can with a good multi-driver, but for listening to music during my commute to and from work these are way more than adequate.

With the upgrades, these are really great. But for the base price, I feel the value level isn't quite what I expected. I'm not sure everyone needs to change out the tips. Some people seem to love the ones from Shure. But I think the cable does need to be replaced if you want a decent experience with these. So all in all, I recommend these, but only if you're willing to spend an extra $30+ over whatever you pay for the actual earphones.
